races.note: OPEN SEAT: REP. DAN NEWHOUSE (R) ANNOUNCED DEC 17, 2025 HE WOULD NOT SEEK A SEVENTH TERM. ⚠ Top-two primary: the two highest finishers advance regardless of party. ✅ Certified Aug 21: McKinney 34.80%, Duresky 29.92% — a Democrat placed second in a district that has not elected one since Jay Inslee in 1992 [Verify — a historical claim from press summaries]. Jerrod Sessler, Trump's 2024 endorsee, ran third at 14.59% and is eliminated.

candidates.name: Amanda McKinney
positions: Commonsense water policy protecting Central Washington farms
Backs Trump on border security and immigration enforcement
Second Amendment, ending DEI, barring trans women from women's sports
differentiators: Yakima County commissioner since 2020
Endorsed by President Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson
Raised over 981,000 dollars by July 15, most in the field
Opposed prolonged COVID shutdowns and vaccine mandates
supporters: Say she pairs America First politics with genuine water and agriculture expertise.
Point to Trump and Johnson endorsements as evidence she can deliver for the district.
Credit her county record of pushing back on federal regulation of farms and dairies.
opponents: Local letters to the editor question what her large financial backers expect in return.
Say she would replace an independent-minded Republican with a straight party-line vote [Verify — structural argument].
Argue a national culture-war focus crowds out district-specific problems like water and labor [Verify — structural argument].

candidates.name: John Duresky
positions: Affordability is the district's top problem
Supports some form of universal health care
Raise Medicare and Medicaid rates for rural hospitals
differentiators: Retired Air Force major, roughly 37 years of federal service
Former project control officer at the Hanford site
Only Democrat among 11 primary candidates
Endorsed by WA State Labor Council and Washington Education Association
supporters: Say a career veteran and federal worker can reach rural voters other Democrats cannot.
Point to his second-place finish as real crossover appeal in a deep-red seat.
Credit town halls in small Klickitat County towns as genuine district outreach.
opponents: Note the seat has not elected a Democrat since 1992 and rates about R+10 [Verify — both figures via aggregators; Cook's own site returned 403].
Say he was heavily outraised in the primary and starts far behind on money.
Argue universal health care is a hard sell in Central Washington [Verify — structural argument].

races.note: FIRST-TERM INCUMBENT MICHAEL BAUMGARTNER (R) DREW 11 CHALLENGERS AND FINISHED UNDER HALF AT 47.40%. ⚠ Top-two primary: party labels are self-declared ballot preferences, not nominations. ✅ Certified Aug 21: Baumgartner 47.40%, Carmela Conroy 18.85%, independent Nate Powell a close third at 16.38%. This is a 2024 rematch; Cook PVI R+5 [Verify — via Ballotpedia and Wikipedia; Cook's own site returned 403].

candidates.name: Michael Baumgartner (incumbent)
positions: Supports the administration's military action against Iran
Aligned with Trump on tariffs and immigration
Sponsored a ban on prediction-market betting on wildfires
differentiators: First-term incumbent, elected 2024
Former state senator and Spokane County treasurer
Sits on Judiciary, Foreign Affairs, and Education and Workforce
Beat Conroy 60.6 percent to 39.3 percent in 2024
supporters: Say three substantive committee seats give Eastern Washington unusual early influence.
Point to a 21-point 2024 win as proof the district is comfortable with him.
Credit locally targeted bills such as his wildfire betting ban.
opponents: The Spokesman-Review has described him as a party-line Trump vote on tariffs and Iran, both unpopular at home.
Note that 11 challengers ran against him and he still finished below 50 percent.
Argue a 47 percent primary showing signals softness in a midterm against the president's party [Verify — structural argument].

candidates.name: Carmela Conroy
positions: Runs on diplomatic and prosecutorial experience over party loyalty
No detailed domestic platform beyond her campaign site could be located [Verify — an absence of located records]
differentiators: Retired U.S. consul general, foreign service 1996 to 2020
Former Spokane County deputy prosecutor
Former chair of the Spokane County Democratic Party, 2022 to 2024
Second run against Baumgartner after losing in 2024
supporters: Say decades of diplomatic service are exactly the check Congress needs during a war.
Argue her 2024 run gave her name recognition a first-time challenger would lack.
Point to an R+5 seat as reachable in a midterm against the president's party.
opponents: Note she lost this same matchup by more than 21 points in 2024.
Say she took under 19 percent in the primary while other Democrats and independents split the rest.
Argue her published platform is thin on the local economy [Verify — structural argument from limited located policy detail].

races.note: INCUMBENT EMILY RANDALL (D) TOOK 58.77% IN THE PRIMARY, MORE THAN HER FOUR OPPONENTS COMBINED. ⚠ Top-two primary: the two highest finishers advance regardless of party. ✅ Certified Aug 21: Randall 58.77%, Republican Teresa Fox 25.54%; Leon Lawson, who prefers the Trump Republican Party, took 9.72%. Cook PVI D+10 [Verify — via Ballotpedia; Cook's own site returned 403].

candidates.name: Emily Randall (incumbent)
positions: Protect and strengthen the Affordable Care Act
Defend reproductive, mental and culturally relevant health care
differentiators: First term; won the open seat in 2024 with 56.8 percent
First queer Latina to serve in the U.S. House
Says she secured 17.9 million dollars for district projects [Verify — self-reported]
Founded and co-chairs the Congressional Ferry Caucus
supporters: Point to federal money delivered for ferries, transit and wastewater across the district.
Say she is a dependable vote for the ACA and reproductive rights.
Credit her attention to Puget Sound Naval Shipyard commuting and workforce needs.
opponents: Note she graded her own first-term work bringing money home only a B-plus.
Say a first-term minority-party member has limited leverage to deliver [Verify — structural argument].
Argue her emphasis fits urban Kitsap better than the rural Olympic Peninsula [Verify — structural argument].

candidates.name: Teresa Fox
positions: Cut federal spending to bring down inflation
Staff and fund rural law enforcement
Fiscal restraint paired with naval readiness
differentiators: Occupational safety professional and emergency manager
Worked in shipyards, naval facilities and at Olympic College
Unanimously endorsed by all six county Republican parties in the district
Runs explicitly as a non-politician against career politics
supporters: Say a shipyard safety career speaks directly to the district's largest employer.
Point to unified backing from every county Republican organization in the district.
Argue voters want a citizen candidate focused on costs and public safety.
opponents: Note she trailed Randall by 33 points in the primary in a D+10 seat.
Say she has never held elected office and no significant fundraising base was located [Verify — an absence of located records].
Argue county-party endorsements do not translate in a district Randall carried with 56.8 percent in 2024.
